description_full: Omega Flex, Inc. manufactures and sells flexible metal hoses, fittings, and accessories in the United States, Canada, and internationally. It offers flexible gas piping for use in residential and commercial buildings; fittings; containment pining; and corrugated copper tubing for use in hospitals, ambulatory care centers, dental, physician and veterinary clinics, laboratories, and other facilities. The company sells its products under the TracPipe CSST, CounterStrike CSST, AutoFlare, DoubleTrac, DEF-Trac, and MediTrac brand names. It serves various markets, including construction, manufacturing, transportation, petrochemical, pharmaceutical, and other industries. The company sells its products through independent sales representatives, distributors, wholesalers, original equipment manufacturers, and direct sales, as well as through its website. The company was formerly known as Tofle America, Inc. and changed its name to Omega Flex, Inc. in 1996. Omega Flex, Inc. was incorporated in 1975 and is based in Exton, Pennsylvania.

financial_summary: Omega Flex, Inc. is a micro-cap industrials business with a $241M market cap on $98M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -8% over the past three years and +1% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.
Returns on capital run at 59% against a 9% cost of capital — a 50-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 61% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $15M in free cash flow — roughly 16 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.16× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 5.7% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 65% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is, and within its sector the business captures 1.6× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

sect: Its 17% operating margin runs 8pp above the Industrials median (9%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.56x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-18.7% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.01 across 544 companies in the universe; the top four hold 9% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the bottom of its 52-week range, 37% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 39% and a beta of 0.90, it moves roughly with the market.
Trading is thin (about $896K a day), below the $1.0M liquidity floor flagged; building a position would move the price.
In past sell-offs it fell 49% in the 2020 crash, 46% in the 2022 bear market and 64% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $23.76 (margin of safety -1%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 21%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $20.40 to $28.37 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Industrials peers: P/FCF 15.7 vs 22.3 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 40% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 6.4% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 8.2% (vs the 8% bar).
The price implies 1.1% annual cash-flow growth.
prof: ROIC of 59% clears the cost of capital of 9.2% by 50pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.43).
It runs a 61% gross margin and converts 16% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.16x.
ROE of 18% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.2x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.3% of revenue on R&D and 0.2% on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $53.2M (22% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 10.1, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 152 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at -7.8% over 3 years, -1.5% over 5 years and 0.5% over 10 years, so the decline is deepening.
At current returns, reinvesting 10% of profits supports about 6.1% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -3.9% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.3x, 1.9% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 14, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders own 65.2%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 32%.
Insiders have only bought over the past year (8 purchases, net $207K bought).
It returns 5.7% a year to shareholders (5.7% in dividends).
It pays out 131% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
people: With about 172 employees, each generates about $571K of revenue, 1.6x the Industrials median, and productivity has risen 4.3% a year.
That works out to $89K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $913K (2x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores poorly (8/10, lower is better).
